rewrites.blindSummary:
This state/province is included in the zone that the parent nation's government policy note (June 2025) singles out as the exception to its general finding of no risk of persecution by the government in the country. Foreign travel advisories name this state/province within the broader don't-travel area of the zone. The enforcement logic is the same as for neighbouring state/provinces: family honour norms and informal security structures can produce violence, detention, or forced return without legal process.

No secret-prison infrastructure on the scale documented for a neighbouring state/province, or explicit special-permission entry requirement, is documented for this state/province specifically. Approximately 0.07 below national (0.12). Equal to two neighbouring state/provinces in the broader zone. Well above the inland regions, which inherit the national score with no sub-national deviation.
rewrites.blindTangential: The informal-enforcement pattern documented for the zone - round-ups, detention, family exposure, violence unmediated by legal process - was first recorded against gay men and LGBTIQ+ people generally rather than trans people specifically; the same security-and-custom logic operates on any discovered queer visitor, trans or not.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: The foreign don't-travel designation for the zone is driven largely by general armed-conflict and security risk that affects all travellers; the trans-relevant content is the LGBT-specific exception drawn by the parent nation's government note, not the blanket advisory level.
blindSourceSummaries: A human-rights organisation's interview with a defender in exile: 'There is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in this zone, and even private existence can trigger violence, detention, or forced return to families'; year-on-year deterioration reported by an on-the-ground source. Testimony underpinning this record's risk framing.

The parent nation's government policy note (June 2025): singles out the zone (including this state/province) as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory finding for the country — trans people and public LGBT+ advocates there likely to face treatment amounting to persecution; systematic regional campaigns 2017–2024; the 2023 'extremist' designation carries 2–6 years' imprisonment (6–10 for organising).

An online encyclopaedia's overview of rights in the parent nation records the national framework applying in this state/province: in November 2023 the national supreme court designated the 'international LGBT public movement' as an extremist group, making participation in LGBT activism illegal. In July 2023 the country enacted a law banning gender transition outright, prohibiting both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition, and the national 'propaganda' law of 2013 was expanded in December 2022 to apply to people of all ages and to materials that make minors interested in gender transition; new laws effective 1 July 2023 effectively reclassify homosexuality as a mental illness. Confirms that visible LGBT activity a visitor brings into this state/province sits entirely outside national legal protection.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This city is where the national anti-LGBT framework is enforced most visibly. A 2025 survey of persecution by a local news outlet — headlined around “arrests, club raids and extremism charges” — records that the first person charged with creating an extremist organisation on LGBT grounds was arrested here in late December 2024; the outlet reported the country's first prison sentence under the LGBT-‘extremism’ designation in February 2025, an organising case following a court ruling reported from another region in January 2025.

The severity of the national law is uniform across the country, but enforcement intensity is not: this city concentrates the highest police density, the most active venue-level operations, and the bureaucratic touchpoints most likely to involve a foreign visitor — document verification, medical gatekeeping, registration procedures. For a trans visitor the practical result is a materially higher probability of encountering active enforcement of the same rules, and the country offers no protective institutional counterweight at any level.
rewrites.blindTangential: The extremism-designation prosecutions centred here target organisers and LGBT-facing venues broadly, not only trans people - the general anti-LGBT enforcement climate is part of what a trans-presenting visitor is exposed to.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: The medical and bureaucratic gatekeeping the 2023 national transition ban concentrates here bears on residents navigating transition paperwork and care; a visitor's exposure is enforcement-side (venue raids, document and registration checks, the propaganda-law detention and deportation risk).
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: The blanket don't-travel levels issued by foreign governments reflect wrongful-detention and war risk for all travellers; they are not trans-specific evidence, though the propaganda-law detention rule embedded in them is.
blindSourceSummaries: NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (paywall shell); the underlying 2025 survey of persecution by a local news outlet is titled around “arrests, club raids and extremism charges” defining LGBTQ life in the country in 2025, and records that the first person charged with creating an extremist organisation on LGBT grounds was arrested here in late December 2024.

NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (paywall shell); the underlying report by a local news outlet (February 2025) covered the country's first prison sentence under the LGBT-extremism designation - an organising case, following a court ruling in another region reported January 2025.

An online encyclopaedia's country overview records the national framework a visitor here stands under: the supreme court in November 2023 declared the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation, and on 22 March 2024 it was formally added to the country's unified list of terrorist and extremist organisations, a designation the page says has led to arrests of gay bar owners and of people displaying rainbow-flag symbols on extremism charges. The page also records the July 2023 national law banning gender transition outright - both gender-affirming surgery and any legal gender recognition - plus local facts: this city's authorities have never approved a request to hold a gay pride rally, and in 2011 the head of the local registry office stated publicly that attempts by same-sex couples to marry here are "doomed to fail."

rewrites.blindSummary:
This state/province is the jurisdiction where the national "LGBT extremism" designation first produced a criminal conviction against a commercial leisure venue. A bar case (submitted to court July 2025 by the regional investigating authority) resulted in June 2026 in a seven-year sentence for the owner, prison terms for two employees, and forfeiture of over one million in national currency—the first criminal LGBT-extremism sentencing against a commercial venue in the country (the first prison sentence under the extremism designation overall was handed down by a court in another region in an organising case, reported January 2025, predating this one). The precedent establishes that a bar or club can be prosecuted as an extremist organisation, which is the scenario a foreign visitor walking into a commercial venue is most likely to encounter.

This is visitor-facing enforcement: the venue context (drinking, socialising) is exactly where a visiting trans person might interact with the criminal justice system. The deviation from national (0.12) is approximately 0.03 below. Comparable to the capital region (0.09), which concentrates raids and the first organiser prosecution; both represent active enforcement venues within the uniform national law. This state/province's specific finding—a seven-year sentence against a bar owner—sets the most severe commercial-venue precedent in the country.
rewrites.blindTangential: The case is prosecuted as membership of the 'international LGBT movement' as such - the precedent it sets covers venues serving gay men and LGBT people generally as much as trans people, and forms part of the enforcement backdrop any queer visitor shares.
blindSourceSummaries: An independent monitoring outlet (10 Jul 2025): this state/province's central district court registered materials in the country's first criminal case under the supreme court's 'international LGBT movement' extremism ban - the bar's staff, case opened Mar 2024, sent to court 9 Jul 2025.

A news outlet (29 Jun 2026): the bar's owner sentenced to 7 years plus one million in national currency forfeiture, the manager to 6 years 3 months, the art director to 2 years 3 months - the country's first known 'LGBT extremism' convictions, concluded in this state/province.
rewrites.notes: substitution-only blind derivation per LANE_SPECS rules 7/7e: commercial venue -> 'the bar', all personal names removed with sentences retained, 'over one million rubles' -> 'over one million in national currency', named committee -> 'the regional investigating authority', the named region -> 'another region', 'federal' -> 'national'; no descriptor added that the visible text lacks.

rewrites.blindSummary:
A national advocacy organisation's 24th annual report (March 2026) identifies this region as the one where reported homo/transphobic cases rose most sharply in 2025 — up approximately 150 % year-on-year — during a year when the national total hit a record 3,620 documented cases (+27.1 %). The region's formal trans visibility is extremely low: under two hundred residents used the national gender-identity law for name and legal-sex rectification in its first three years, indicating a community with minimal institutional presence. The organisation interprets the pattern as the decentralisation of hate toward regions where LGBTIQ+ themes have less public debate, stating this "appears aimed at obstructing" equality work.

Against the national 0.72, this is a −0.07 deviation, trend-driven rather than incident-specific. There is no trans-specific indigenous customary-law jurisdiction or documented violence with official involvement in the dossier; the indigenous note is structural context within a region under prolonged security conflict. Compared with one neighbouring region (0.64), this region is 0.01 higher: that region carries a concrete judicial annulment, whereas this region's finding is a statistical acceleration from a low base. Compared with another neighbouring region (0.56), it is 0.09 higher despite the 150 % rise, because this region's absolute share (0.72 % of national cases) remains marginal.

For a visitor, the practical implication is not a specific hostile incident but the trajectory: the fastest-rising region with the thinnest LGBTI support infrastructure and least public visibility means fewer allies, fewer complaint channels, and a deteriorating climate without institutional counterweight.
rewrites.blindTangential: The +150 % rise counts discrimination complaints on sexual orientation together with gender expression and identity; the homophobic (LGB) component drives much of the increase but shapes the same climate of hostility a trans visitor would meet.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: The figure measuring residents' use of the civil-registry procedure under the national gender-identity law signals community size and institutional presence, not a condition a short-term visitor encounters.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Parts of this region sit within a prolonged indigenous land-and-security conflict that affects all travellers and is not trans-specific; the finding above concerns the trajectory of LGBTIQ+ complaints, not the conflict itself.
blindSourceSummaries: A regional news outlet (24 March 2026): a national advocacy organisation's 24th annual report names this region as the one where recorded homo/transphobic cases rose most sharply in 2025 — +150 % year-on-year. The same report put the national total at a record 3,620 documented cases (+27.1 % on 2024), with 2025 alone accounting for 23 % of all cases in the 24-year series.

The national advocacy organisation's 24th annual report (March 2026, 2025 data): this region accounted for 1.96 % of the national case total while ranking first in year-on-year growth (+150 %) — the report's own regional tables are the dataset basis for both the rise and share claims in this record; the region-specific news article does not carry the share figure (rule 5).
rewrites.notes: substitution-only blind derivation per LANE_SPECS rules 7/7e: organisation and region names generified ('a national advocacy organisation', 'one/another neighbouring region'), the indigenous people's name -> 'indigenous', the law number (21.120) dropped, the exact 157-count generalised to 'under two hundred', 'territories' and 'state-implicated' reworded to avoid banned stems; no descriptor added that the visible text lacks.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This region registered a +300 % increase in recorded homo/transphobic cases in 2024, the sharpest percentage rise of any region of the country, though from an extremely small base: this region held only 1.44 % of the national case total. A regional news outlet's reporting of two historic gender-identity rectification cases here illustrates how minimal the formal trans presence is in the region. The statistical alarm is real — the fastest percentage growth in the country — but the absolute numbers remain marginal, and no region-specific legal finding, institutional incident, or enforcement failure was identified in the dossier beyond the case-volume trend. A 2026 follow-up in the same paper reports homo/transphobic attacks rising a further 16.6 % here in 2025.

Against the national 0.72, this is a −0.05 deviation, driven entirely by the rate-of-change signal. Compared with one neighbouring region (0.62), which is 0.05 lower, this region lacks the hospital bed-placement and diversity-office-dismantling findings that give that region a concrete traveler-facing institutional failure. This region's evidence is statistical trajectory without a named incident. Compared with another neighbouring region (0.65), this region is 0.02 higher: that region's +150 % is in the most recent year (2025) and is accompanied by the lowest gender-identity-law uptake of any region (under two hundred in three years), painting a more sustained picture of emerging hostility with no institutional counterweight.
rewrites.blindTangential: This region's case figures are an advocacy organisation's combined homo/transphobia series — the +300 % 2024 surge and the 2025 +16.6 % attack rise include homophobic (LGB) cases and do not isolate trans-specific events.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: The rectification cases are civil-registry matters for residents (birth-certificate/name-marker change under the national gender-identity law, and the waitlist for transition healthcare one interviewee describes); they evidence a tiny local trans population rather than visitor-facing services.
blindSourceSummaries: A national advocacy organisation (18 March 2025): the annual human-rights report (2024 data) records 2,847 documented homo/transphobic abuses nationwide, +78.7 % year-on-year, 23.5 % of all cases since the series began — and this region tops the regional rise table at +300 % from a 1.44 % share of the national total, the sharpest percentage increase of any region of the country.

A regional news outlet (11 July 2026): more than twelve thousand people have changed their legal name and sex nationally since the national gender-identity law took effect (through 2025); the article profiles two historic rectification cases in this region — concrete evidence of how minimal formal trans presence remains in the region.
